title: Files & Paths
subtitle: open(), read/write modes, with statement, and pathlib
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Programs need persistent storage — configuration, data, logs. Reading and writing files is a fundamental I/O operation.
whyItExists.solution: Python's built-in open() function and the pathlib module provide a clean API for file I/O. The with statement ensures files are always properly closed.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Reading config files, writing logs, processing CSV/JSON data files, working with any file on disk.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: For large datasets, use pandas. For databases, use sqlite3 or SQLAlchemy. For network data, use requests.

explainModes.beginner: open() is like opening a physical file cabinet drawer. You specify which drawer (filename), whether you're just reading or also writing, and when you're done you must close it. The with statement closes it automatically.
explainModes.simple: Modes: 'r' (read, default), 'w' (write/overwrite), 'a' (append), 'x' (create-new, fails if exists), 'b' (binary — add to any: 'rb'/'wb'). with open(path, mode) as f: — auto-closes. Read: f.read() (all), f.readline(), f.readlines(), or iterate with for line in f. Write: f.write(text). pathlib.Path for OS-independent path handling.
explainModes.standard: Text mode uses the system encoding (usually UTF-8). Always pass encoding='utf-8' explicitly to be safe. f.read() loads the entire file into memory — fine for small files, use iteration for large files. writelines() writes a list without adding newlines — you must include \n yourself. Mode 'w' truncates the file first. Mode 'a' always writes at the end.
explainModes.technical: open() returns a file object with a file descriptor (OS handle). Python's io module underlies all file I/O — text files are BufferedReader/BufferedWriter wrapped in TextIOWrapper. Buffering is on by default — flush() or close() pushes buffered data to disk. Memory-mapped files (mmap module) for large file access without reading the whole file. The with statement calls __enter__/__exit__ on the file object — context manager protocol.
explainModes.deepDive: pathlib.Path returns Path objects with / operator for joining: base / 'subdir' / 'file.txt'. Path.glob() and Path.rglob() for pattern matching. Path.stat().st_size, .st_mtime for metadata. shutil for copying, moving, deleting directories. tempfile for secure temp files. fileinput module to edit files in-place. csv and json modules handle structured text formats.

content.code:
# Read the entire file
with open('notes.txt', 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    content = f.read()
print(content)

# Read line by line (memory-efficient)
with open('notes.txt', 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.strip())   # strip() removes the \n

# Read all lines into a list
with open('notes.txt', 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    lines = f.readlines()   # ['line1\n', 'line2\n', ...]

# Read one line at a time
with open('notes.txt', 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    first = f.readline()    # first line (including \n)
    second = f.readline()   # second line

# Write (creates or OVERWRITES the file)
with open('output.txt', 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    f.write('Hello, World!\n')
    f.write('Second line\n')

# Append (adds to the end, doesn't erase)
with open('output.txt', 'a', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    f.write('Third line\n')

# Write multiple lines at once
lines = ['apple\n', 'banana\n', 'cherry\n']
with open('fruits.txt', 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    f.writelines(lines)     # no \n added automatically!

# Or use join + write (cleaner)
fruits = ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']
with open('fruits.txt', 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    f.write('\n'.join(fruits))

from pathlib import Path

# Create path objects
home = Path.home()                  # C:\Users\Prashant or /home/prashant
docs = home / 'Documents'          # join with /
file = docs / 'notes' / 'todo.txt'

print(file)              # full path
print(file.name)         # todo.txt
print(file.stem)         # todo
print(file.suffix)       # .txt
print(file.parent)       # .../notes

# Check existence
print(file.exists())
print(file.is_file())
print(file.is_dir())

# Read/write with pathlib
Path('output.txt').write_text('Hello!', encoding='utf-8')
content = Path('output.txt').read_text(encoding='utf-8')

# Find files
for py_file in Path('.').glob('**/*.py'):  # all .py files recursively
    print(py_file)

# Create directories
Path('data/logs').mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

questions.question: What is the difference between open modes 'w' and 'a'?
options: 'w' is for binary; 'a' is for text
questions.explanation: 'w' (write) opens a file for writing — if it exists, it TRUNCATES (erases) the content first. 'a' (append) also creates the file if needed, but always writes at the END, preserving existing content.

faq.q: What happens if I forget to close a file?
faq.a: The file stays open consuming a file descriptor until the garbage collector reclaims it (or the program exits). On Windows this can prevent other programs from opening the file. Always use 'with open(...) as f:' — it closes the file automatically even if an exception occurs.

faq.q: How do I read a JSON file?
faq.a: import json; with open('data.json', 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f: data = json.load(f). This gives you a Python dict/list. To write: json.dump(data, f, indent=2). json.loads()/json.dumps() work with strings instead of files.
